content: Early diagnosis of leptospirosis is crucial for improving the effectiveness of antimicrobial therapy and for recognizing outbreaks promptly. Nucleic acid and antigen detection tests have shown potential for facilitating early diagnosis of this condition. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of these diagnostic methods. The objective of the review was to determine the diagnostic accuracy of nucleic acid and antigen detection tests in identifying symptomatic leptospirosis in humans. To achieve this, electronic databases such as MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and regional databases were searched up to July 6, 2018, without restrictions on language or publication date. The review included diagnostic cross-sectional and case-control studies that utilized nucleic acid and antigen detection methods in individuals suspected of having systemic leptospirosis. The reference standards used were the microscopic agglutination test (MAT), either alone or in combination with culturing or other serological tests. Studies were excluded if the controls were healthy individuals or if there was insufficient data to calculate sensitivity and specificity. Data extraction was performed independently by at least two reviewers. The quality of the studies was assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool, which evaluates the risk of bias. Sensitivity and specificity values were calculated for each study, and meta-analyses were conducted when appropriate. For tests with a single positivity threshold, a bivariate model was used, while a hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) model was applied for tests with multiple thresholds. Potential sources of heterogeneity, such as timing of the test, disease prevalence, blood sample type, primers or target genes, and real-time PCR visualization methods, were explored using meta-regression models. The review included 41 studies that evaluated nine diagnostic tests: conventional PCR, real-time PCR, nested PCR, PCR performed twice, loop-mediated isothermal amplification, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), dot-ELISA, immunochromatography-based lateral flow assay, and dipstick assay. These studies involved 5,981 participants, of whom 1,834 had leptospirosis and 4,147 did not. Methodological quality was often poorly reported, and the reference standard was generally considered to have a high risk of bias. The use of frozen samples in many studies limited the applicability of the findings. Meta-analyses were conducted for conventional PCR and real-time PCR on blood products. The pooled sensitivity of conventional PCR was 70% (95% CI: 37% to 90%), and the pooled specificity was 95% (95% CI: 75% to 99%). When studies with a high risk of bias in the reference standard were excluded, the pooled sensitivity increased to 87% (95% CI: 44% to 98%), and the pooled specificity rose to 97% (95% CI: 60% to 100%). For real-time PCR, a summary receiver operating characteristic curve was generated. At a specificity of 85%, the sensitivity was 49% (95% CI: 30% to 68%). At 90% specificity, the sensitivity was 40% (95% CI: 24% to 59%), and at 95% specificity, the sensitivity was 29% (95% CI: 15% to 49%). The median specificity of real-time PCR on blood products was 92%. However, no direct comparison studies were available to formally compare the diagnostic accuracy of conventional PCR and real-time PCR. In studies analyzing conventional PCR on blood products, only three out of 15 reported the timing of sample collection, which ranged from 1 to 7 days after symptom onset. For real-time PCR, nine out of 16 studies reported sample collection timing, ranging from 1 to 19 days post-symptom onset. Specificity for conventional PCR was found to be lower in settings with high leptospirosis prevalence. Other investigations into heterogeneity did not reveal statistically significant associations. Two studies suggested that both conventional PCR and real-time PCR might be more sensitive when blood samples are collected early in the disease course. The results for other diagnostic tests were described narratively rather than quantitatively. The authors concluded that the findings of the review should be interpreted with caution due to substantial variability in the accuracy of PCR and real-time PCR across studies, as well as variability in leptospirosis prevalence. The clinical utility of these tests depends on regional factors, including disease prevalence, factors influencing test accuracy, and the implications of test results. There is insufficient evidence to determine which nucleic acid or antigen detection test is the most accurate. Preliminary evidence suggests that PCR and real-time PCR may be more sensitive when performed on blood samples collected early in the disease, but further research is needed to confirm this.
